strategy_title: Adding N-boundary mask and eviction_policy caused regression
strategy_description: Adding a full 2D boundary mask to the B-matrix load (K & N dimensions) and adding eviction_policy='evict_first' to both A and B loads produced a 0.867x regression. All profiling metrics are essentially unchanged (Duration: 47.68→48.13 µs, Mem Busy: 70.32→70.99%, L1 hit rate: 1.59%→1.59%, bank conflicts: 55.37→55.39% speedup potential), indicating the change had no meaningful effect on the bottlenecks (shared memory bank conflicts, low occupancy) and introduced a small overhead. The root bottleneck — 7.9-way shared memory bank conflicts causing 55%+ speedup potential — remains completely unaddressed by mask changes or eviction policies.
slow_pseudocode:
# B load with K-only mask
b_mask_k = rk[:, None] < K
b = tl.load(b_ptrs, mask=b_mask_k, other=0.0)
# A load without eviction policy
a = tl.load(A + xindex, mask=a_mask, other=0.0)
fast_pseudocode:
# B load with full 2D mask + eviction policy
b_mask = (rk[:, None] < K) & (offs_b_n[None, :] < N)
b = tl.load(b_ptrs, mask=b_mask, other=0.0, eviction_policy='evict_first')
# A load with eviction policy
a = tl.load(A + xindex, mask=a_mask, other=0.0, eviction_policy='evict_first')
applicable_when: Never — this specific combination did not help and caused a slight regression
do_not_apply_when: When the dominant bottleneck is shared memory bank conflicts (7.9-way, 55%+ speedup potential) and low occupancy (12.5% theoretical). Adding boundary masks and eviction_policy='evict_first' to streaming loads does not address bank conflicts or register pressure, and the wider 2D mask computation adds marginal overhead. L1 hit rate remained at 1.59% before and after, confirming eviction policies had no measurable effect on cache behavior.
framework_notes: In Triton, eviction_policy='evict_first' on tl.load is intended to prevent L1/L2 pollution for streaming data. However, when L1 hit rate is already near 0% (1.59%), the cache is not being used for these loads regardless, making the eviction hint a no-op in practice. The 2D boundary mask (rk[:,None] < K) & (offs_b_n[None,:] < N) adds a predicate computation per load but does not change the access pattern or bank conflict structure.

strategy_title: Adding N-dimension mask to B load causes regression
strategy_description: Adding a combined K+N boundary mask to the B-matrix tl.load (b_mask = b_mask_k & b_mask_n) and augmenting the A-matrix mask with an M-dimension guard produced a 0.867x regression. The profiling metrics are nearly identical before and after — elapsed cycles increased from 71367 to 72035, memory throughput dropped slightly from 380 to 377 GB/s, and all occupancy/warp statistics remained flat — indicating the mask additions added minor overhead without resolving the underlying bank conflict or occupancy bottlenecks. The SharedMemoryConflicts (7.9-way, ~55% speedup potential) and UncoalescedSharedAccess (66% excessive wavefronts) rules remained completely unchanged, confirming the masks did not address the structural access pattern problem.

When SharedMemoryConflicts and UncoalescedSharedAccess are the dominant bottlenecks, mask changes do not address the root cause (access stride pattern). When BLOCK_N > N_actual, the fix for out-of-bounds accumulation requires restructuring the access pattern (e.g., using actual N in tile sizing or transposing the load), not just masking.

The masks did not change the underlying shared memory bank conflict pattern because the conflict arises from the stride of the access (stride_bn=144), not from out-of-bounds loads. The correctness issue (max_diff ~58) persisted across all prior iterations and was NOT resolved by this mask addition, suggesting the root cause lies elsewhere (possibly in the accumulator initialization, the dot product layout, or the output store logic).
